A.translation: [343] GALEN, WHOM ONE MUST PURGE, AND WITH WHAT CATHARTICS, AND WHEN. Those who have healthy bodies are troublesome to purge; for they become dizzy and suffer griping, and the purgation proceeds with difficulty in them, and in addition to this they are, moreover, quickly exhausted. All these things come about because the cathartic drug strives to draw the humour proper to it, and, being at a loss for it, melts down the blood and the flesh, in order that it may draw from these what is proper to it.

But those who are still healthy, yet would fall ill [344] if they were not evacuated, one must anticipate by evacuating them at the onset of spring, either through phlebotomy, if they are seized by plethoric diseases, or through purgation, if by those arising from corruption. We, at any rate, have by means of such evacuation prevented, for many years indeed, both podagra and arthritis that was beginning and had not yet produced tophi about the joints from coming about. In the same way we have put a stop to apoplexy, epilepsy, melancholy, and other such chronic affections in many people through the aforesaid evacuation. For some, then, it is beneficial that the phlegmatic humours be evacuated, for others the bitter-bilious, for others the melancholic, for others the serous residue, according to the nature of the affections that habitually occur in them. For instance, a certain man is seized by melancholy every year if he is not purged, and I purge him not only in spring but also in autumn. So too I likewise evacuate a certain woman every year at the onset of spring, who had a cancerous condition in the breast, which I cured by evacuating her strongly with a drug that purges black bile.

And if ever [345] the purgation is omitted, a pain arises in her deep within. In another man I cured an incipient elephas at first by phlebotomy and purgation, and each year thereafter a single purgation suffices for him too; but if it is left out, the affection at once gives signs of itself. Such diseases, then, require a purgation of the black humours; epileptic, apoplectic and asthmatic diseases, of the phlegmatic humours; arthritic diseases, those accompanied by much heat, of the bitter-bilious humours, and those with cold swellings, of the phlegmatic ones. Another man, who was always seized by tertian fevers in the season of summer, has now for many years not had a fever, being purged of yellow bile by us in anticipation at the end of spring. For it is better to evacuate such persons in this way, just as it is better for epileptics, arthritics and melancholics, and all the others who are ill on account of thick humours, to be evacuated at the onset of spring.

One must first thin and cut the thick and viscous humours, and open up the passages through which these are transferred and drawn, before the cathartic drugs, if the [346] purgation is to be best in every respect, and especially in the case of those taking hellebore. For the intensity of the convulsive retchings, which expels the humours that are wedged in the affected parts in a manner hard to loosen and in this respect benefits the chronic affections, will accomplish this more easily when they have been thinned beforehand. But if they neglect these things, the purgations turn out troublesome, sometimes accompanied by gripings and certain vertigos, much nausea and bad pulse, faintness and distress. In those who are about to take hellebore, one must first make trial of their nature, to see how it stands with regard to upward purgations, that is, those through vomiting. Let the trial be made by means of emetic drugs, such as are moderate. For if he does not appear to be purged easily, one must not lead such a person on to hellebore without preparing him beforehand. This could be done both through these very [emetics] and through repeated vomitings, the person who is going to take the hellebore being habituated to vomit readily. And it would be done better also by moistening the bodies beforehand. They are moistened beforehand by more abundant nourishment and by rest.

The matter of [347] rest, then, is clear. For just as exercises are of a nature to dry, so rest, which is quiet and absence of exercise, is of a nature to preserve the moistures. But nourishment is not of a nature to moisten simply by being more abundant, but rather that nourishment which is without any strong quality, that is, neither astringent nor acrid nor salty nor bitter. We have sometimes given radishes with oxymel, having fixed into them for a whole day and night sprigs of white hellebore; and such a purgation from hellebore would be a weak one. Those who have a narrow (στέρνον ἔχοντε) thorax, and for this reason also a compressed one, happen to be most unsuited to purgations by means of emetic drugs, both the others and especially those by means of white hellebore; for in them some vessel among those in the respiratory organs ruptures. One must also evacuate the bitter-bilious humour upward, and the phlegm downward; sometimes, however, the reverse, if the phlegmatic humour should have gathered in the stomach and the bitter-bilious in the intestines; the melancholic humour, however, always downward.

It is written in the Aphorisms of Hippocrates concerning the seasons: in summer purge [348] the upper cavities, in winter the lower. And what is analogous to the seasons must be considered in the case of regions, dividing them by heat and cold; and so too in the case of ages. And indeed habit also is no small part in the indication of evacuation. For those accustomed to vomit bear with less distress the purgations through the upper cavity, whereas those unaccustomed bear them not without danger, and more so in the case of hellebore. And it is fitting to consider also the form of the disease. For in the case of the phlegmatic dropsy one needs a drug that is a drawer of phlegm, first through the lower belly, then through vomits, then through apophlegmatisms; for since what is in excess is extended throughout the whole body, we shall employ all the evacuations. But in the case of the ascitic dropsy we shall give one of the hydragogue drugs, just as in the case of the icteric one of the cholagogue drugs. And one must purge out the bile of these too in many ways, both upward and downward, and through the urine and the palate and through the nostrils.

So too, if the melancholic humour is in excess, as in melancholia and cancer and [349] elephas, we give the drug that evacuates black bile, while we purge epilepsies with phlegm-drawing drugs. From which it is clear that the condition of the disease indicates both the humour to be evacuated and the place through which one must evacuate it. Indeed, in the case of those with inflammation in the liver too, once they have been concocted, we carry out the evacuation: through the lower belly, when the affection arises in its concave parts, and through urine, when in its convex parts. So too in the other cases you will examine both the humour that is in excess and the affected place, from which, as from a cause, the disease sets out. For these will indicate to you both the humour to be evacuated and the manner of the evacuation and the place through which it must be evacuated, and, in addition to all these, the right moment. For at the beginning you will evacuate the serous and thin humours; but you will await concoction in the case of the thick and viscous ones, such as by nature are the humour of phlegm and that of black bile.

And from the paroxysms too you will have an indicator for the indication of the manner of evacuation, making the evacuations from the upper parts during the paroxysms, and from the [350] lower parts during the so-called remissions. For spontaneous evacuations too bring benefit in this way, many patients vomiting and bleeding through the nostrils during the paroxysms, while during the remissions urine and stools are excreted. One must especially be on guard against the time of the paroxysmal and critical days whenever you attempt to purge downward copiously. For when the inclination of the humours has come to be upward, the power of the purging drug will be impeded. In those who are already ill, in chronic diseases one must always await concoction, whereas in acute ones, when the matter is turgid, it is possible to administer a purgative drug at the beginning; and this very thing one must do with great caution and circumspection. For there is no small danger in an acute disease of administering a purgative badly, because all purging drugs are hot in their powers, whereas fever, insofar as it is fever, on its own account requires not at all the drying and heating things, but rather those most contrary to them, the moistening and cooling ones. Accordingly, purgation is not taken up by us for the sake of the fiery heat itself.

For we know that this [heat], so far as depends on itself, is [351] harmed; rather, it is for the sake of the humours that produce it. It is necessary, therefore, that the benefit arising from the evacuation of the troublesome humours be greater than the harm which the body must of necessity suffer from the cathartic drugs. And the benefit is greater if the harmful humour is evacuated both without distress and in its entirety. In order for this to come about, one must first consider carefully whether the patient is suitably disposed for such a purgation. For those who are in a state resulting from many indigestions or from viscous or thick foods, and likewise those whose hypochondria are tense and distended with wind, or are excessively hot and fiery, or in whom there is also some inflammation of the viscera in that region—all these are unsuitable for purgations. It is necessary, therefore, that these conditions be absent, and that the patient's humours be as free-flowing as possible, that is, thin and partaking less of any viscosity, and that the passages through which the purgation is going to take place be opened wide. For these are precisely the things that we ourselves prepare in advance whenever we are about to purge someone.

But in acute diseases, right at the beginning—that is, on the first day, or not beyond the second—when we are going to employ [352] purgations at the time the humour is in turgor (ὀργᾷ), such a preparation cannot be carried out, unless perhaps one should have the opportunity to have unmixed melikraton made and given, having boiled in it some hyssop, or thyme, or origanum, or goat's-origanum, or pennyroyal, or some other of the things that thin in this way; so that with good reason we shall seldom have need of drugs at the beginning in acute diseases, because neither are the offending humours often in turgor at the beginning, nor, even if this is the case, would the patient be suited to the purgation, nor indeed does he afford us a suitable opportunity to prepare him. The humours are said to be in turgor when, having come into a more violent motion and flowing across from parts to parts, at the beginning of the disease they trouble the person, causing pain and nausea and tickling irritation and not permitting him to be at rest. Such humours, then, it is fitting to evacuate, that is, those that are in motion and movement and flux. But those already fixed in some one part one must neither set in motion by any other remedy nor purge with drugs before they have been concocted. For then we shall also have nature assisting the evacuation.

For it is seen, after the concoctions, both separating the [353] humours and casting off the superfluity, at which very time crises also occur. But when it is moving completely, there is no need at all of medication; when, however, it acts more moderately and more weakly, we must ourselves supply what is lacking by administering drugs, so that the evacuation of the troubling humour may come about from both together, nature thrusting it out and the drug drawing it. One must know that the fluxes of the humours from one part to another at different times occur seldom; for the most part they are at rest and remain in some one part, in which they are also concocted throughout the whole time of the disease until its resolution. So when the affection is not only acute but also accompanied by a most violent fever, one must be cautious about the giving of the cathartic drug, and most of all when one is inexperienced in the nature of the patient. Some are by nature hard to purge, while some upon a small draught of a drug are purged copiously. So when the fever is not violent, and you are experienced in the nature of the patient, you will proceed to the giving of the drug, using black hellebore or one of those of similar character, among which is also the preparation made with colocynth, which they customarily call hiera.

[354] And since it is prepared in various ways, the version that has taken hellebore but does not contain scammony is the best laxative drug. After the cathartic has been taken it is beneficial to sip ptisane afterwards, as Hippocrates says. For the cathartic drug itself, being small in quantity, arrives at the bottom of the belly, but along its passage the gullet and whatever is high up around the stomach, partaking not only of the quality of the purging agent but also of its substance adhering in the passage, is greatly harmed. The juice of ptisane sipped afterwards is therefore useful, as being able to wash off and sweep downwards what has been plastered on in the passage, and to temper and alter the quality of the drug that has settled into the parts. For these reasons, then, upon the drinking of the cathartic drug he bids one sip ptisane afterwards. But once the purgation has begun to take place, he no longer wishes ptisane to be given, taking care lest the action of the purging drug be dissipated.

Sometimes, however, the belly does not excrete when a purgative has been given, either because of the peculiarity [355] of the patient's nature or because of the smallness of the quantity of the drug given. Often, too, hard faeces wedged in one of the intestines, which could have been evacuated by means of a clyster before the purging drug was given, prevents the evacuation. It is also possible that, when the nature has directed its impulse toward the urine, the cathartic accomplishes nothing. Sometimes, when purging drugs fail, some of them, besides doing no harm at all to the body, even become nourishment for the living being, while others turn toward the destructive and poisonous. And since all purging drugs harm the belly, and especially its mouth, because it is most sinewy and most sensitive, the admixture of fragrant substances was devised, so that their power might not touch the body of the belly alone and unmixed. The seeds that are mixed in must be such as are naturally able both to blunt their harmfulness and not to hinder their activity, being of an attenuating and incisive power, so as both to cut the thick humours and to open up and unstop the passages through which they are evacuated.

It is necessary, moreover, [356] that the cathartics which are mixed together be of like kind with one another and in no respect at variance. Their variance arises not when the one, say, evacuates bile and the other phlegm—for both can be evacuated in the same manner—but when the one is of such a nature as to set the purgation in motion immediately, the other only long after its administration. For in this way the evacuation becomes irregular, when they are administered together. And I call it irregular when, at the point where it already seems to be ceasing, the beginning of another evacuation arises again.

B.translation: [343] GALEN: WHOM ONE MUST PURGE, WITH WHAT CATHARTICS, AND WHEN. It is a laborious matter to purge those who have their bodies in a healthy state; for they become dizzy and suffer gripings, the purgation proceeds with difficulty in them, and besides this they also quickly become faint. All these things happen because the cathartic drug strives to draw its proper humour, and, through lacking it, colliquates the blood and the flesh, so that it may draw from them what is proper to it.

Those, however, who are still healthy but would fall ill [344] if they were not evacuated, one must evacuate in advance at the onset of spring, either by phlebotomy, if they are prone to the plethoric diseases, or by purgation, if to those arising from corruption. We at any rate, by such evacuation, have for many years now prevented both podagra and arthritis that was beginning, and had not yet produced concretions (pōroi) about the joints, from developing. In the same way we have, through the aforementioned evacuation, put a stop in many people to apoplexy, epilepsy, melancholy and other such chronic affections. For some, then, it is beneficial that the phlegmatic humours be evacuated, for some the bitter-bilious, for some the melancholic, and for some the serous residue, according to the substance of the affections that customarily befall them. For example, a certain man is seized by melancholy every year unless he is purged, and I purge him not only in spring but also in autumn. So too I likewise evacuate every year at the onset of spring a certain woman who has a cancerous condition in the breast, whom I cured by evacuating her vigorously with a drug that purges black bile.

And if the purging is ever not administered, [345] a deep-seated pain arises in her. In another man I cured elephas in its beginning, at first by phlebotomy and purging; and for him too a single purging each year suffices thereafter, but whenever it is omitted the affection at once shows its signs. Such diseases, then, require purging of the black humours; the epileptic, apoplectic and asthmatic ones require purging of the phlegmatic humours; and of the arthritic ones, those accompanied by much heat require purging of the bitter-bilious humours, and those with cold swellings of the phlegmatic. Another man, who was always seized by tertian fevers in the summer season, has now not had fever for many years, because he was purged of pale bile by us in advance, at the end of spring. For it is better to evacuate such people in this way, just as it is better for the epileptics, the arthritics, the melancholics and all others who are ill because of thick humours to be evacuated at the onset of spring.

One must first attenuate and cut the thick and viscous humours, and open up the passages through which these are transferred and drawn, before the cathartic drugs, if the [346] purgation is to turn out best in every respect, and especially in those who take hellebore. For the violence of the spasmodic retchings, which expels the humours wedged fast, and hard to dislodge, in the affected parts, and in this way benefits the chronic affections, will accomplish this more easily if these humours have been attenuated beforehand. But if they neglect these things, the purgations turn out troublesome, sometimes with gripings and some vertigo, much nausea and bad pulse, faintness and discomfort. In those who are about to take hellebore one must first test the nature, how it stands with regard to purgations upwards, that is, those by vomiting. Let the test be made by means of emetic drugs, those that are moderate. For if he does not appear to be purged easily, one ought not to bring such a person to hellebore without preparing him beforehand. This could be done both by these themselves and by continual vomitings, the person who is going to take the hellebore having been accustomed to vomit readily. And it could be done better also by moistening the bodies beforehand. They are moistened beforehand by more abundant food and by rest.

The matter [347] of rest, then, is clear. For as exercises naturally dry, so rest, which is quiet and absence of exercise, naturally preserves the moistures. Food, however, does not moisten simply by being more abundant; that food moistens which is without a strong quality, that is, neither astringent nor acrid nor salty nor bitter. We have sometimes given radishes in oxymel, having fixed shoots of white hellebore into them for a whole day and night, and such a purging from hellebore would be a weak one. Those who have the thorax narrow and for this reason also compressed are the most unsuitable of all for purgations by means of emetic drugs, both the others and above all those by means of white hellebore. For in them some one of the vessels in the respiratory organs ruptures. One must also evacuate the bitter-bilious humour upwards and the phlegm downwards. There are times, however, when it is the reverse, if a phlegmatic humour has collected in the stomach and a bitter-bilious one in the intestines. The melancholic humour, however, must always be evacuated downwards.

It is written in the Aphorisms of Hippocrates concerning the seasons: 'In summer purge [348] the upper cavities, in winter the lower.' And one must consider what corresponds to the seasons in the case of regions, distinguishing them by heat and coldness; and so too in the case of the ages. Moreover, habit is no small factor in the indication for evacuation. For those accustomed to vomiting bear purgations through the upper belly with less distress, whereas the unaccustomed do so not without danger, and more so with hellebore. One ought also to consider the form of the disease. For in phlegmatic dropsy there is need of a drug that draws off phlegm, first through the lower belly, then by vomiting, then by apophlegmatisms. For since what is in excess is spread through the whole body, we shall employ all the evacuations. In ascitic dropsy we shall give one of the water-drawing drugs, just as in jaundiced patients one of the bile-drawing drugs. And in these too one must purge out the bile in many ways, upward and downward, and through the urine and the palate, and through the nostrils.

So too, if the melancholic humour is in excess, as in melancholia, cancer and [349] elephantiasis, we give the drug that evacuates black bile; and cases of epilepsy we purge with phlegm-drawing drugs. From this it is clear that the state of the disease indicates both the humour that is to be evacuated and the place through which one must evacuate it. Indeed, with inflammations in the liver as well, once they have been concocted, we carry out the purging: through the lower belly when the affection arises in its concave parts, and through the urine when it is in the convex parts. In the same way you will examine, in the other cases too, both the humour that is in excess and the affected place, from which, as from a cause, the disease takes its start. For these will indicate to you the humour to be evacuated, the manner of the evacuation, the place through which the evacuation must be made, and, in addition to all these, the right moment. At the beginning you will evacuate the serous and thin humours. But you will wait for concoction in the case of the thick and viscous ones, which is the nature of the humour of phlegm and that of black bile.

From the paroxysms, too, you will have a guiding mark for the indication of the mode of evacuation, making the evacuations from the upper parts during the paroxysms, and from the [350] lower parts during the so-called remissions. For this is also how spontaneous evacuations bring benefit: during the paroxysms many people vomit and bleed from the nostrils, while in the remissions urine and alvine discharges are excreted. One must above all be on guard about the time of the paroxysmal and critical days whenever you undertake to purge copiously downwards. For when the inclination of the humours has turned upwards, the power of the purging drug will be impeded. In those who are already ill, in chronic diseases one must always await concoction, but in acute ones, when [the matter] is turgid, it is possible to administer drugs at the outset; and this very thing must be done with much caution and circumspection. For there is no small danger in purging badly in an acute disease, because all purging drugs are hot in their powers, whereas fever, insofar as it is fever, according to its own definition requires not only not drying and heating things, but even their most contrary ones, the moistening and cooling. Therefore purgation is not employed by us even for the sake of the fiery heat itself.

For we know that this heat, so far as it itself is concerned, [351] is harmed by it; rather, purgation is employed for the sake of the humours that produce it. The benefit arising from the evacuation of the troublesome humours must therefore be greater than the harm which the body necessarily suffers from cathartic drugs. And the benefit is greater if the harmful humour is evacuated both without distress and in its entirety. For this to happen, one must first consider carefully whether the patient is in a suitable condition for such a purgation. For those who come from many indigestions, or from viscous or thick foods, and likewise those whose hypochondria are tense and inflated, or are excessively hot and fiery, or who have some inflammation of the viscera there: all these are unsuited to purgations. These conditions must therefore be absent, and the patient's humours must be as free-flowing as possible, that is, thin and having little share of any viscosity, and the passages through which the purgation is to take place must be opened up. For these are the very things that we too prepare in advance whenever we intend to purge someone.

But in acute diseases, right at the outset, that is, on the first day or not later than the second, when we intend to employ [352] purgations because the humours are turgid, such preparation cannot take place. The exception is if one should perhaps have the opportunity to give unmixed honey-water to be made, with some hyssop or thyme or origanum or goat's origanum or pennyroyal boiled in it, or some other of the things that attenuate in this way. So it is reasonable that in acute diseases we shall seldom have need of drugs at the outset. For the offending humours are not often turgid at the beginning, nor, even if this is the case, would the patient be suited to purgation; indeed he does not even afford us a suitable opportunity to prepare him. The humours are said to be turgid when, having come into more violent motion and flowing over from part to part, they trouble the person at the beginning of the disease, causing pain, causing nausea, gurgling, and not allowing him to keep at rest. Such humours, then, it is proper to evacuate, that is, those in motion, transport and flux. But those already fixed in some one part one must neither stir with any other remedy nor purge with drugs before they have been concocted. For at that time we shall also have nature assisting the evacuation.

For nature is seen, after the concoctions, both separating the [353] humours and setting aside the superfluity, at which time crises also occur. But when nature is moved perfectly, there is no need of purging with drugs; when it acts more moderately and more weakly, we ourselves must supply what is lacking by administering drugs, so that the evacuation of the troublesome humour may come about from both, nature thrusting it away and the drug drawing it. One must know that the shiftings of the humours, now into one part and now into another, occur rarely; for the most part they are at rest and remain in some one part, in which they are also concocted throughout the whole time of the disease until its resolution. When, therefore, the affection is not only acute but is also accompanied by a very violent fever, one must be cautious about giving the cathartic drug, and especially when one is unacquainted with the nature of the patient. Some people are by nature hard to purge, while others are purged copiously upon a small draught of the drug. When, therefore, the fever is not violent and you are acquainted with the nature of the patient, you will proceed to the giving of the drug, using black hellebore or one of those of similar character, among which is also the preparation made with colocynth; they customarily call it hiera.

[354] Since it is prepared in various ways, the one that has taken in hellebore but does not contain scammony is a most excellent drug for purging downwards. After the purgative has been taken, it is beneficial to sip some ptisan after it, as Hippocrates says. For the cathartic drug itself, being small in quantity, reaches the bottom of the belly. But along its passage the gullet (stomachos), and as much of the stomach as lies high up, take up not only the quality of the purging agent but also its substance, which settles in the passage, and they are greatly harmed. The juice of the ptisan, therefore, is useful when sipped afterwards. It can wash off what has stuck in the passage and sweep it downward, and it can temper and alter the quality of the drug that has settled in the parts. For these reasons, then, he bids one sip ptisan after the drinking of the cathartic drug. But once the purgation has begun to take place, he no longer wishes ptisan to be given, taking care lest the action of the purging drug be weakened.

Sometimes the belly does not evacuate when a purgative has been given, either because of the peculiarity [355] of the patient's nature or because of the smallness of the drug given. Often, too, hard faeces wedged in one of the intestines prevent the evacuation; these can be evacuated by a clyster before the purging drug is given. It is also possible for the cathartic to achieve nothing when nature has directed its impulse towards the urine. Sometimes, when purging drugs fail, not only do they do the body no harm but they even become nourishment for the animal; others, however, turn towards what is destructive and deleterious. Since all purging drugs injure the stomach, and above all its mouth, because it is most nervous and most sensitive, the admixture of fragrant substances was devised, so that their power should not touch the body of the stomach alone and unmixed. The seeds that are mixed in must be such as naturally both blunt their harmfulness and do not hinder their action, being of a thinning and cutting power, so as both to cut the thick humours and to open up and unstop the passages through which they are evacuated.

And it is necessary [356] that the cathartics that are mixed be of like kind with one another and in no respect at variance. Their discord arises not when the one, say, evacuates bile and the other phlegm (for both can be evacuated in the same manner), but when the one naturally sets the purgation in motion at once, and the other long after its administration. For in this way the evacuation becomes irregular, when they are administered together. I call it irregular when, while it already seems to be ceasing, the beginning of another evacuation occurs again.
